title: Correlation Nanoscopy Using AFM and Nano-optical Imaging and Spectroscopy Techniques
content: Advances in nano-optical techniques have fundamentally transformed this landscape, providing researchers with the ability to image and analyze samples at unprecedented resolution, far beyond the limits imposed by conventional light microscopy. Nano-optical techniques, such as near-field scanning optical microscopy (s-SNOM), nano-FTIR, AFM-IR, and tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), have evolved over the past few decades. They break the diffraction limitation of the spatial resolution of the optical microscopy, simultaneously enhancing the sensitivity level. A scattering type Scanning Near-Field Optical Microscopy (s-SNOM) uses a sharp tip to scan the surface of a sample while exciting and detecting optical signals that are confined to the tip-sample interaction area. By operating in the near-field regime, s-SNOM can achieve spatial resolution on the order of 10–20 nm, far exceeding conventional optical methods. This resolution is defined exclusively by the apex shape of the AFM probe and is not dependent on the wavelength of utilized light. nano-FTIR extends the principles of s-SNOM with the broadband infrared spectroscopy, enabling vibrational spectroscopy and chemical identification at the nanoscale. This capability to resolve chemical composition at the nanoscale has been pivotal for fields such as materials science and biology, enabling researchers to investigate the molecular structure of polymers, biomolecules, and thin films with extraordinary detail.
